## Family placement

Hindi is New Indo-Aryan and belongs to the Indo-Iranian branch of Indo-European. Its history is not a direct, uninterrupted “Sanskrit became Hindi” line: Middle Indo-Aryan varieties (including Prakrits and Apabhraṃśa traditions) intervene, and reconstruction depends on comparative evidence. Hindustani describes a shared colloquial base from which standardized Hindi and Urdu developed distinct registers and scripts.

**Proposed root:** Proto-Indo-Aryan (with deeper Proto-Indo-Iranian comparison) — 3200–3800 BP, using 1950 CE as the conventional BP origin. The qualifying point estimate is 3500 BP. Confidence: moderate for Vedic attestation horizon; lower for exact proto-stage dating. This date concerns the stated ancestor; it is not an age claim for the modern language. 

**Siblings and comparisons:**
- Urdu (closely related standard register in the Hindustani continuum; Perso-Arabic script)
- Punjabi (Northwestern Indo-Aryan)
- Gujarati (Western Indo-Aryan)
- Bengali (Eastern Indo-Aryan)
- Marathi (Southern Indo-Aryan)

Do not flatten distant relatives and immediate sister groups into a single branching level.

## Chronology and evidence

The Rigvedic language is traditionally dated to the second millennium BCE and transmitted orally; later Sanskrit and Middle Indo-Aryan records document successive stages. Hindi as a named modern standard is much more recent than its Indo-Aryan ancestry. Nineteenth- and twentieth-century print, education, and state policy helped standardize Khari Boli-based Hindi in Devanagari, alongside Urdu standardization in Perso-Arabic script.

**Dating statement:** The Ṛgveda is conventionally placed around 1500 BCE within a wider c.1500–500 BCE composition horizon. It was transmitted orally, and surviving written records are much later. Proto-Indo-Aryan is reconstructed; the Vedic textual horizon is not a securely dated Proto-Indo-Aryan split.

Keep three clocks separate: (1) reconstructed ancestor age, (2) earliest surviving written attestation, and (3) emergence of a standardized modern variety. They answer different questions. A lack of early writing is not evidence that a language did not exist.

## Sound history

Hindi has a contrastive inventory including dental/retroflex stops, aspirated/unaspirated stops, and nasal contrasts; phonetic realization varies by region and register. Schwa deletion is a major phonological process: the inherent schwa represented by many consonant letters is absent in some lexical environments, and ordinary spelling does not mark every deletion. Do not equate orthographic akshara counts with phonetic syllables.

For reliable sound-change claims, identify the source stage, daughter branch, conditioning environment, and counterexamples. Orthographic similarity alone cannot establish cognacy or sound correspondence. Reconstructed segments use an asterisk and remain hypotheses.

## Syllables, prosody, and syntax

Hindi commonly uses SOV order, postpositions, split ergativity in perfective transitive clauses, and agreement patterns conditioned by case marking and construction. Syllables allow complex onsets in loans and limited codas; vowel length and nasalization contrast. Prosodic phrasing and stress are not written with routine accent marks in standard Devanagari.

The descriptive labels here are broad summaries, not templates for every dialect or genre. Compare attested forms by date and register; syntax may change while a writing convention remains conservative. Phonological syllables, script units, aksharas, and Unicode grapheme clusters are distinct analytical units.

## Script, Unicode, diacritics, and glyphs

Modern Standard Hindi is written in Devanagari, a Brahmi-derived, left-to-right abugida with inherent vowel, dependent vowel signs, virama, and conjunct formation. Devanagari developed through northern Indian script stages including Gupta and Nāgarī; its headline, consonant bodies, and attached vowel signs are shaped by the abugida design and evolving manuscript/print hands. Braj and other prose traditions used Devanagari before the 19th-century Sanskritized Khari Boli standard; Kaithi remained important in administrative handwriting, while print and language politics increasingly privileged Devanagari Hindi. Related Urdu is normally written in a Perso-Arabic script. Script differentiation does not imply unrelated colloquial grammars.

**Unicode model:** Devanagari U+0900–U+097F, with extensions in separate blocks. Consonant + VIRAMA (U+094D) may form conjuncts; vowel signs attach to consonants and some render before the base consonant while encoded after it.

| Sample | Code points | Note |
|---|---|---|
| हिन्दी | U+0939, U+093F, U+0928, U+094D, U+0926, U+0940 | Hindi (Unicode sequence; shaping changes visual placement) |
| कि | U+0915, U+093F | KA + short-I sign; visual sign appears before consonant |
| ् | U+094D | VIRAMA / halant |
| ड़ | U+0921, U+093C | DDA + nukta |

**Subscripts:** Conjunct forms are produced by consonant sequences with virama and shaping; they are not a general inventory of subscript letters. Some conjunct glyphs are ligatures or half-forms.

**Diacritics and combining marks:** Nukta U+093C extends consonant distinctions; candrabindu U+0901 and anusvara U+0902 mark nasalization/nasal phenomena depending on word and convention. Vedic marks and transliteration diacritics need separate treatment from everyday Hindi spelling.

**Glyph strokes and layout:** Unicode stores logical character order, not the visual leftward placement of short-i matra or the stroke order of handwritten aksharas. Grapheme segmentation and font shaping follow Devanagari-specific rules.

Unicode encodes characters, not the complete historical calligraphic or palaeographic process. Record source form, normalization, transliteration, and rendering assumptions separately.

## Family placement

Khmer belongs to Austroasiatic, specifically the Khmeric grouping in a classification whose internal subgrouping continues to be refined. Khmer is not a Tai language, despite long contact with Thai and Lao. Distant Austroasiatic comparisons such as Mon, Vietnamese, and Khasi do not imply immediate sisterhood; use branch-qualified trees.

**Proposed root:** Proto-Austroasiatic — 3000–4500 BP, using 1950 CE as the conventional BP origin. The qualifying point estimate is 3500 BP. Confidence: contested model; low confidence in exact chronology and homeland. This date concerns the stated ancestor; it is not an age claim for the modern language. 

**Siblings and comparisons:**
- Vietnamese (Vietic branch; distant Austroasiatic relative)
- Mon (Monic branch; distant relative)
- Khasi (Khasic branch; distant relative)
- Pearic languages (neighboring Austroasiatic group; not Khmer dialects)

Do not flatten distant relatives and immediate sister groups into a single branching level.

## Chronology and evidence

Old Khmer is attested in inscriptions from the early seventh century CE, making the epigraphic record direct evidence for historical Khmer rather than a proxy for Proto-Austroasiatic. Inscriptions preserve language variation across time and place. The transition from Old to Middle and Modern Khmer is a sequence of changes, not a sharp replacement date.

**Dating statement:** Interdisciplinary proposals combine comparative linguistics and archaeological evidence; dates are hypotheses, not direct attestations.

Keep three clocks separate: (1) reconstructed ancestor age, (2) earliest surviving written attestation, and (3) emergence of a standardized modern variety. They answer different questions. A lack of early writing is not evidence that a language did not exist.

Modern Khmer has a complex vowel system and register contrasts linked historically to changes in the voicing of stops and the loss/reorganization of phonation contrasts. The chronology and phonetic details of register development remain debated. Khmer spelling is morphologically and historically conservative in places, so a grapheme sequence should not be treated as a narrow phonetic transcript.

## Syllables, prosody, and syntax

Khmer has predominantly analytic morphology, uses particles and word order for grammatical relations, and generally follows SVO order in neutral clauses. Syllables can have complex onsets, a restricted set of codas, and register-sensitive vowel realizations. Khmer orthographic syllables and Unicode grapheme clusters do not always map one-to-one to spoken syllables.

The descriptive labels here are broad summaries, not templates for every dialect or genre. ## Script, Unicode, diacritics, and glyphs

Khmer script is a Brahmi-derived abugida, transmitted through South Indian script traditions (often described via Pallava), and is historically attested in inscriptions by the early seventh century CE. Pre-Angkorian and Angkorian epigraphy shows dated regional letterform variation. Consonant series condition dependent-vowel readings; subscript consonants form clusters. In Unicode, COENG is an invisible encoding control followed by a consonant, not a standalone Khmer letter. Tie claims about individual glyph changes to inscriptional palaeography rather than assume a single unchanged model.

**Unicode model:** Khmer U+1780–U+17FF; Khmer Symbols U+19E0–U+19FF. U+17D2 KHMER SIGN COENG combines with a following consonant to form subscript-consonant sequences in shaping.

| Sample | Code points | Note |
|---|---|---|
| ភាសាខ្មែរ | U+1797, U+17B6, U+179F, U+17B6, U+1781, U+17D2, U+1798, U+17C2, U+179A | Khmer-language phrase; the coeng sequence is visible in Khmer |
| ្ | U+17D2 | COENG sign |
| ក | U+1780 | KA |
| ា | U+17B6 | AA dependent vowel sign |

**Subscripts:** In the Unicode model, U+17D2 COENG (an invisible encoding control, not a Khmer letter taught as a standalone sign) followed by a consonant encodes a subscript consonant form. Preserve code-point order and let a Khmer-capable shaping engine form the glyph.

**Diacritics and combining marks:** U+17C9 and U+17CA are Khmer register-related signs (MUUSIKATOAN and TRIISAP); vowel signs are dependent signs, and combining marks have script-specific ordering. Do not normalize away distinctions or insert generic combining marks by visual guess.

**Glyph strokes and layout:** Consonant series, inherent vowels, dependent vowels, and coeng clusters interact. Glyph placement is shaping behavior, not encoded stroke recipes; fonts and rendering engines matter.

Unicode encodes characters, not the complete historical calligraphic or palaeographic process. Record source form, normalization, transliteration, and rendering assumptions separately.

## Sources

## Family placement

Linear B is a writing system; the language it records is Mycenaean Greek, the earliest directly written Greek dialect. Greek belongs to Hellenic within Indo-European. Mycenaean is compared with later Greek varieties including Arcado-Cypriot, Attic-Ionic, Aeolic, and Doric groups. Linear A is a different, undeciphered script tradition and should not be called Greek merely because Linear B adapted some signs from it.

**Proposed root:** Proto-Greek / early Greek dialect continuum — 3400–4000 BP, using 1950 CE as the conventional BP origin. The qualifying point estimate is 3600 BP. Confidence: moderate for chronology of Greek presence and linguistic identification; exact Proto-Greek split date is modeled. This date concerns the stated ancestor; it is not an age claim for the modern language. 

**Siblings and comparisons:**
- Attic-Ionic Greek (later branch/dialect group)
- Aeolic Greek
- Doric and Northwest Greek
- Arcado-Cypriot Greek (closest comparison group in many classifications)
Linear A belongs in the related-script comparison, not in the Greek language sibling list.

Do not flatten distant relatives and immediate sister groups into a single branching level.

## Chronology and evidence

Linear B is attested in administrative archives from the Late Bronze Age, roughly the fifteenth through twelfth centuries BCE, with chronology depending on site and tablet context. Tablets were often short-lived palace records and baked during destruction events; they are not representative literary corpora. The 1952 decipherment by Michael Ventris, with John Chadwick’s linguistic collaboration, established the language as Greek.

**Dating statement:** Linear B tablets from the second millennium BCE directly record Mycenaean Greek; comparative Greek dialect history reconstructs earlier Proto-Greek ancestry.

Keep three clocks separate: (1) reconstructed ancestor age, (2) earliest surviving written attestation, and (3) emergence of a standardized modern variety. They answer different questions. A lack of early writing is not evidence that a language did not exist.

## Sound history

Linear B is an open-syllable logo-syllabary with signs broadly representing V, CV, and selected clusters. It poorly represents Greek consonant codas and several contrasts; scribes omit final consonants or use conventional spellings with “dummy” vowels. For example ti-ri-po can represent tripos. Sign values, spelling conventions, and dialect phonology must be kept analytically separate.

For reliable sound-change claims, identify the source stage, daughter branch, conditioning environment, and counterexamples. Orthographic similarity alone cannot establish cognacy or sound correspondence. Reconstructed segments use an asterisk and remain hypotheses.

## Syllables, prosody, and syntax

Mycenaean Greek has inflectional morphology inherited into later Greek, but tablet genre constrains syntax: inventories and ration lists favor compressed administrative formulae. The syllabary records syllabic chunks, not syllables transparently in the phonological sense, because codas and clusters are underrepresented. Stress and vowel quantity are not systematically marked by Linear B signs.

The descriptive labels here are broad summaries, not templates for every dialect or genre. Compare attested forms by date and register; syntax may change while a writing convention remains conservative. Phonological syllables, script units, aksharas, and Unicode grapheme clusters are distinct analytical units.

## Script, Unicode, diacritics, and glyphs

Linear B descends from/adapts the earlier Linear A sign system for Greek. It combines syllabograms with ideograms and numerical signs, written primarily left-to-right on clay tablets. The script was deciphered, but some sign values and readings remain disputed or unknown. Editorial transliterations use hyphens between signs; a notation like pa₂ is a Latin scholarly label with a subscript numeral, not a special Linear B glyph.

**Unicode model:** Linear B Syllabary U+10000–U+1007F; Linear B Ideograms U+10080–U+100FF; Aegean Numbers U+10100–U+1013F. Unicode characters represent encoded signs; editorial transliteration systems are separate.

| Sample | Code points | Note |
|---|---|---|
| 𐀀 | U+10000 | Linear B Syllable B008 A |
| 𐀁 | U+10001 | Linear B Syllable B038 E |
| 𐀒 | U+10012 | Linear B Syllable B001 DA |
| 𐀀𐀀 | U+10000, U+10000 | Two encoded signs; no implicit hyphen or word boundary |

**Subscripts:** Subscript numerals in transliterations (e.g. pa₂) disambiguate sign labels or readings; they are Latin editorial characters, typically U+2082, not native subscripts in Linear B.

**Diacritics and combining marks:** Linear B does not mark Greek accentuation or vowel length in a way comparable to later Greek orthography. Diacritics used in scholarly Greek forms belong to transliteration/editorial practice. Preserve original sign sequence separately from normalized transliteration.

**Glyph strokes and layout:** Paleographic variation among scribes is essential evidence. Unicode encodes sign identity but does not specify wedge/stroke order, tablet orientation, line layout, or archaeological damage.

Unicode encodes characters, not the complete historical calligraphic or palaeographic process. Record source form, normalization, transliteration, and rendering assumptions separately.
